passages.t: The king comes gentle, on a donkey and a colt
passages.happening:
Jesus and his disciples come near Jerusalem, to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives. He sends two disciples into the village ahead. There they will find a donkey tied up, “with her colt beside her” (verse 2). They are to untie both and bring them. If anyone asks, they are to say that the Lord needs them.

Matthew stops to say why: “This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet” (verse 4). Then he quotes it: “See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (verse 5).

The disciples lay their cloaks on the animals, and Jesus sits on them. A huge crowd spreads cloaks and branches on the road. The crowds in front and behind shout, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” and “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!”

When he enters Jerusalem, the whole city is stirred and asks, “Who is this?” (verse 10). The crowds answer, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.”
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this scene too (Mark 11:1-11), and the note on Mark 11 explains Bethany, the cloaks spread for a king, the branches, and the cry ‘Hosanna’, a Hebrew word that first meant ‘Save us, please’. Here are the things Matthew does differently.

Matthew names the prophecy. This is one of about ten places where he says that something happened ‘to fulfill’ what a prophet said. He wants his readers to see that Jesus is Israel's promised king, arriving the way Scripture said he would.

Matthew has two animals, a donkey and her colt, where Mark, Luke and John have one. The hard question below looks at why.

Matthew's crowd shouts ‘Hosanna to the Son of David’. That makes the welcome plainly a welcome for the promised king of David's line. Two blind men at Jericho have just called Jesus by that title (20:30).

Branches and ‘Hosanna’ already belonged together for Jewish worshippers. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, says that at the Feast of Tabernacles the people shook their palm branches at the words of Psalm 118:25, “O LORD, save us, we pray” (Sukkah 3:9).

Only Matthew says the whole city was ‘stirred’. The Greek verb is the one used for an earthquake. Matthew uses it again when the earth shakes as Jesus dies (27:51) and when the guards shake with fear at the empty tomb (28:4). Jerusalem is shaken, and asks, ‘Who is this?’ The crowd's answer, ‘the prophet from Nazareth’, is true, but Matthew's readers know it is not the whole answer.
passages.ot:
The quotation joins two prophets. The first words, ‘Say to the Daughter of Zion’, echo Isaiah: “Say to Daughter Zion: See, your Savior comes!” (Isaiah 62:11). The rest is Zechariah: “See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). Matthew keeps the king's gentleness and leaves out ‘righteous and victorious’. Jesus called himself ‘gentle and humble in heart’ (11:29).

The next verse in Zechariah says what kind of king this is: “I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be broken. Then He will proclaim peace to the nations” (Zechariah 9:10). A war horse would have said the opposite.

The crowd's words come from Psalm 118:26: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.”
passages.hard:
Did Matthew put Jesus on two animals at once? Zechariah 9:9 is Hebrew poetry. In Hebrew poetry the second half of a line often says the first half again in other words, so ‘on a donkey, on a colt’ most likely means one animal. Mark, Luke and John have one. Matthew has two, and says Jesus sat ‘on them’ (verse 7). Many critics conclude that Matthew misread the poetry, invented a second animal to match it, and left a picture that skeptics find absurd. The objection is old and fair.

Others answer in several ways. Some point out that Matthew knew the Scriptures well, and think he was following a Jewish way of reading in which every phrase of Scripture counts. Others think Matthew reports a real detail. Mark says no one had ever ridden the colt (Mark 11:2), and an unbroken young animal would go more calmly with its mother beside it. On that view ‘He sat on them’ means on the cloaks, or that he rode one while the other came along. Already in the second century, Justin Martyr knew both animals and read them as a picture: the donkey used to the harness stood for the Jewish people, who had the law, and the unbroken colt for the Gentiles, the non-Jews, and both would believe (Dialogue with Trypho 53).

Christians who hold a high view of Scripture are found on more than one side here, and these notes do not choose. What all four Gospels agree on is the point: Jesus came into Jerusalem as Zechariah's humble king, not on a war horse.
passages.asks: The city asked, ‘Who is this?’ It is still the right question. The crowd's answer was true as far as it went. Ask how you would answer, and whether your answer is as small as theirs. And ask what kind of king you want: one who comes with chariots, or one who comes gentle, to make peace.

passages.t: The temple, the blind and the lame, and the children
passages.happening:
Jesus goes into the temple courts and drives out all who are buying and selling there. He overturns the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. He tells them, “It is written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’ But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’” (verse 13).

Then the blind and the lame come to him in the temple, and he heals them. The chief priests and scribes see these wonders, and they hear children shouting in the temple courts, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” They are indignant. “Do You hear what these children are saying?” they ask. Jesus answers with a psalm. Then he leaves the city and spends the night in Bethany.
passages.hearers:
The note on Mark 11 explains the temple courts, the money changers and the doves. Pilgrims had to change their money because the temple took its yearly tax in one kind of silver coin, and doves were the offering of the poor (Leviticus 5:7). Matthew tells the scene more briefly, with some changes.

In Mark, Jesus looks around the temple on the day he arrives and comes back the next day. In Matthew he acts on the day he rides in. Matthew also stops the quotation at ‘a house of prayer’, without Mark's ‘for all the nations’.

Only Matthew tells what happened next. The blind and the lame came, and Jesus healed them right there in the temple courts. People with such conditions were often kept at the edges of worship. An old saying from David's day ran, “The blind and the lame will never enter the palace” (2 Samuel 5:8), and the law did not let a priest who was blind or lame offer at the altar (Leviticus 21:18). Jesus clears out the traders, and the people who had been kept at a distance come in and are made well.

Only Matthew tells of the children too. They pick up the crowd's cry and shout it in the temple courts. Children had no public voice, and the leaders are angry to hear such words from them. Jesus is glad to hear them.
passages.ot:
Jesus joins two prophets, as in Mark. Isaiah promised, “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7). Jeremiah stood in the temple gate and warned people who sinned all week and then ran to the temple as if it would keep them safe: “Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?” (Jeremiah 7:11).

His answer to the leaders comes from Psalm 8:2: “From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise.” In the psalm the praise belongs to God. Jesus accepts it for himself.

Malachi had promised that “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple” (Malachi 3:1).
passages.hard:
What was Jesus doing? Christians and scholars read the scene in a few ways. Some see a cleansing: Jesus protests against greed and unfair trade in God's house and calls it back to prayer. Some see a sign of judgment: like Jeremiah, Jesus acts out the end of the temple, and the fig tree in the next scene points the same way. Matthew adds a third picture. Once the trade is gone, the house fills with healing and with children's praise. These readings can overlap, and many hold more than one.

John tells of Jesus clearing the temple near the start of his work (John 2:13-22), while Matthew, Mark and Luke put it in the last week. Some think it happened twice. Others think John placed one event early for reasons of his own. These notes do not settle it.

This was not Jesus attacking his own people's faith. He was a Jew speaking inside Israel's own tradition, as Jeremiah had, about the house of his Father. And the people who came to him in the temple, the blind, the lame and the children, were Jewish worshippers.
passages.asks: When Jesus cleared the temple, the people who had been kept out came in. Ask who finds it hard to come near God in your church: the disabled, the poor, the noisy child. Ask whether anything in you, or in your church, is in their way. And notice who praised Jesus that day: not the experts, but children.

passages.t: The fig tree withers at once
passages.happening:
Early the next morning, on his way back into the city, Jesus is hungry. He sees a fig tree by the road and goes up to it, but finds nothing on it except leaves. “May you never bear fruit again!” he says. And at once the tree withers.

The disciples are amazed. “How did the fig tree wither so quickly?” they ask. Jesus answers that if they have faith and do not doubt, they will not only do what was done to the fig tree. Even if they say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. “If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story in two parts, with the temple scene in between and a day's wait before the disciples see the dry tree (Mark 11:12-14, 20-25). He also tells his readers that it was not the season for figs. Matthew tells it in one piece, after the temple, and the tree withers on the spot. The note on Mark 11 explains why many readers take the story as a sign about the temple.

Near Jerusalem fig trees put out their leaves in spring, around Passover. Writers differ on whether small early figs come just before the leaves or with them, but a tree in full leaf could look as if it promised something to eat. This tree had the look of fruit and nothing else.

Matthew's readers had heard about fruit from the start. John the Baptist told the Pharisees and Sadducees, “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance” (3:8). Jesus said a tree is known by its fruit (7:16-20). And in the parable at the end of this chapter, the vineyard is given to those who will produce its fruit (verse 43).

Many readers think ‘this mountain’ meant the temple mount, in view across the valley from the road. Others read ‘moving mountains’ simply as a common picture for doing what seems impossible.
passages.ot:
The prophets used the fig tree as a picture of God's people. Hosea remembered how God first saw Israel “as the firstfruits of the fig tree in its first season” (Hosea 9:10). Jeremiah, warning of judgment, said there would be “nor figs on the tree, and even the leaf will wither” (Jeremiah 8:13). Micah grieved that there was “no early fig that I crave” (Micah 7:1).

The prophets also acted out their messages. Jeremiah smashed a clay jar in front of the city's leaders to show what was coming (Jeremiah 19).
passages.hard:
Why would Jesus curse a tree for having no fruit? Skeptics have long pressed the question, and it is fair: the tree did nothing wrong. Most Christian readers take the story as an acted parable, a sign done in public. Matthew puts it the morning after the temple scene, and the prophets had used the fig tree as a picture of God's people. So the tree with leaves and no fruit is read as a picture of a temple busy with worship but bearing no fruit for God. Some scholars think a parable Jesus told, like the one in Luke 13:6-9, was later told as an event. Others take it as an event that Jesus meant as a sign.

One caution matters a great deal. For centuries some Christians read the withered tree as God cursing the Jewish people. That reading fed contempt and cruelty. Jesus and his disciples were Jews, and so were the crowds who welcomed him. The sign is aimed at the temple leadership in that hour, not at a people.

Does verse 22 promise that we will get anything we ask for if we believe hard enough? Some teachers have said so, and have told people that unanswered prayer means weak faith. That has hurt many who prayed for a sick child or a broken marriage and did not see it healed. Most Christian traditions read the promise in the light of the whole Gospel. Jesus taught his disciples to pray ‘your will be done’ (6:10), and in Gethsemane he prayed, “Yet not as I will, but as You will” (26:39). So the promise is read as a call to bold prayer to a Father who can do anything, not a tool for making God do what we want.
passages.asks: Leaves without fruit looks like life from far away. Ask where your faith might be all leaves: busy, visible and religious, but bearing little of the love, honesty and mercy God looks for. The question is for every reader, not for someone else. Then ask whether there is something you have stopped asking God for because it seems impossible.

passages.happening:
Jesus comes back to the temple courts and begins to teach. The chief priests and the elders of the people come up to him. “By what authority are You doing these things?” they ask. “And who gave You this authority?”

Jesus says he will answer if they answer one question first. “What was the source of John’s baptism? Was it from heaven or from men?” (verse 25). They talk it over. If they say ‘from heaven’, he will ask why they did not believe John. If they say ‘from men’, they are afraid of the people, who all hold that John was a prophet. So they answer, “We do not know.” Jesus replies that neither will he tell them by what authority he does these things.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this exchange in almost the same words (Mark 11:27-33), and the note on Mark 11 explains it. The chief priests and the elders were the leaders in charge of the temple. A teacher from Galilee had just overturned its business, so their question is a fair one from where they stood.

In Matthew, Jesus is teaching when they interrupt him. ‘These things’ means everything since the day before: the entry, the tables overturned, the healings, the children's praise.

Jesus' question is not a dodge. It is the answer, if they will see it. John had pointed to Jesus. If John's work came from God, so does the authority of the one John announced. ‘From heaven’ was a respectful Jewish way of saying ‘from God’.

Notice what the leaders weigh. Not whether John was sent by God, but what each answer would cost them.
passages.ot: John came as the messenger promised by Malachi, who would prepare the way (Malachi 3:1). Matthew said John was the one Isaiah spoke of, a voice crying in the wilderness (3:3, from Isaiah 40:3), and Jesus said John was the Elijah who was to come (11:14). Now the Lord has come to his temple, and its leaders say they do not know.
passages.asks: The leaders could not answer because they were weighing what was safe, not what was true. Ask whether you ever do the same: deciding what you believe about Jesus by what it would cost you, or by what others would think.

passages.t: Two sons: the one who said no, and went
passages.happening:
Jesus goes on: “But what do you think?” A man has two sons. He tells the first, ‘Son, go and work today in the vineyard.’ The son says, ‘I will not.’ But later he changes his mind and goes. The father says the same to the second son. ‘I will, sir,’ he says. But he does not go.

“Which of the two did the will of his father?” Jesus asks. “The first,” they answer. Then Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you” (verse 31). John came to them in a righteous way, and they did not believe him, but the tax collectors and prostitutes did. And even after they saw it, they did not change their minds and believe.

This story is found only in Matthew.
passages.hearers:
This is the first of three stories Jesus tells the leaders who have just questioned his authority. All three are about a vineyard or a feast, and all three are about who says yes to God and who does not.

The first son is rude. He says no to his father's face. The second is polite and calls his father ‘sir’. The hearers would expect the polite son to be the good one. Jesus turns it round. What counts is not the right words but going to the vineyard.

Tax collectors worked for the rulers and were known for taking more than was due. Prostitutes were among the most shamed people in the land. Both were counted far from God. Yet Luke also remembers that tax collectors were among those who came to John and were baptized (Luke 3:12; 7:29-30). The religious leaders, who would have said yes to God with every prayer, did not.

‘Before you’ uses a Greek verb that means ‘to go ahead of’. Some readers hear in it a door that is not yet shut. The leaders are being overtaken, but they could still follow.
passages.ot: The prophets knew both sons. Ezekiel promised that a wicked man who turns back can live: “But if a wicked man turns from the wickedness he has committed and does what is just and right, he will save his life” (Ezekiel 18:27). And God warned Ezekiel about people who listen politely and change nothing: “They hear your words but do not put them into practice” (Ezekiel 33:32).
passages.hard:
The old manuscripts tell this parable in more than one form, and some English Bibles differ. In the form printed by most modern Bibles, the first son refuses and then goes, and the leaders answer ‘the first’. Some manuscripts reverse the order of the sons, so that the answer is ‘the last’. A few have the first son refuse and go, and yet have the leaders answer ‘the last’, which would make them answer wrongly. Editors have argued for each form. All of them make the same point: doing the father's will is what counts, not saying the right words.

Does Jesus mean that the leaders are shut out? He does not say that. He says that others are going in ahead of them, and he names the reason: they saw people change their lives and still did not change their minds. The warning is real. So is the open door.
passages.asks: Which son are you? Many people who grew up in church have said ‘I will, sir’ to God for years and never gone to the vineyard. Others said no to God loudly, and later turned around. Ask whether your yes to God is a word or a life. And if you once said no, hear that it is not too late to go.

passages.t: The tenants of the vineyard, and the stone the builders rejected
passages.happening:
Jesus tells another parable. A landowner plants a vineyard, puts a wall round it, digs a winepress and builds a tower. He rents it to tenants and goes away. At harvest he sends his servants to collect his share of the fruit. The tenants seize them. They beat one, kill another, and stone a third. He sends more servants, and the tenants do the same. Last of all he sends his son. ‘They will respect my son,’ he says. But the tenants say, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and take his inheritance.’ They throw him out of the vineyard and kill him.

“What will he do to those tenants?” Jesus asks. The leaders answer: “He will bring those wretches to a wretched end,” and rent the vineyard to others who will give him his share (verse 41).

Jesus quotes a psalm: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Then he says, “Therefore I tell you that the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people who will produce its fruit” (verse 43). Whoever falls on this stone will be broken, and the one it falls on will be crushed.

“When the chief priests and Pharisees heard His parables, they knew that Jesus was speaking about them” (verse 45). They want to arrest him, but they are afraid of the crowds, who hold him to be a prophet.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this parable too (Mark 12:1-12), and the note on Mark 12 explains the tenant farmers and the song of the vineyard in Isaiah 5. As soon as Jesus described the wall, the winepress and the tower, his hearers knew the story was about God and his people. The vineyard itself is not the villain. The tenants who were put in charge of it are.

Matthew tells it with some differences. The servants come in groups, and one is stoned, as prophets had been. The son is thrown out of the vineyard first and then killed, where Mark has him killed first. Some readers think Matthew is thinking of how Jesus would be led out of the city to die (compare Hebrews 13:12).

In Matthew the leaders pass the sentence themselves. Jesus asks what the owner will do, and they answer. It is like the moment when the prophet Nathan told King David a story, David condemned the man in it, and Nathan said, “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7).

Only Matthew has verse 43. It speaks of ‘fruit’, a word Matthew has used from his first chapters (3:8; 7:16-20; 21:19). And only Matthew names who heard it: ‘the chief priests and Pharisees’, who knew Jesus was speaking about them. The crowds, Jewish pilgrims, were on Jesus' side.

Some old manuscripts do not have verse 44, about falling on the stone. It is very like Luke 20:18, and some editors think it was copied in from there. Most modern Bibles print it, some with a note.
passages.ot:
Isaiah's song begins, “My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill.” The owner “built a watchtower in the middle and dug out a winepress as well” (Isaiah 5:1-2). Then the song asks the hearers to judge: “What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it?” (Isaiah 5:4). And it explains itself: “For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7). In Isaiah the vineyard is torn down. In Jesus' story the vineyard is kept, and given new tenants.

The stone saying is Psalm 118:22-23, the psalm the crowds sang as Jesus rode in: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes.”

The crushing stone recalls two more passages. Isaiah warned that people would trip over God's stone: “Many will stumble over these; they will fall and be broken” (Isaiah 8:15). And Daniel saw a stone, “cut out, but not by human hands,” that struck a great statue and broke it in pieces (Daniel 2:34). That stone stood for the kingdom God would set up, which “will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44).
passages.hard:
Does verse 43 mean that God has rejected the Jewish people and given their place to the church? For centuries many Christians read it that way. The view that the church has replaced Israel in God's purposes is called supersessionism, or ‘replacement’ theology. That reading of this parable was used to justify contempt and worse toward Jews. The passage does not say it, and this site rejects that use plainly.

Look at what Matthew says. Jesus says ‘taken away from you’ to the chief priests and elders who questioned him (verse 23), and Matthew adds that the chief priests and Pharisees knew he meant them (verse 45). The crowds listening, all of them Jews, held him to be a prophet. The tenants are the vineyard's keepers, not the vineyard, and the vineyard is not destroyed. It is a warning to people given charge of God's people, not a verdict on a nation.

Readers differ on who the ‘people who will produce its fruit’ are. Some read it as the new leaders Jesus was gathering, the Twelve, all of them Jews, who would sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (19:28). Some read it as Israel renewed around its Messiah, into which the nations are now gathered. Many read it as the church, Jews and Gentiles together.

Christians also differ on how Israel and the church are related. Many hold that the church, Jews and Gentiles together, is one people of God, grafted onto Israel's olive tree, and that God has not let go of the Jewish people. Many of these expect a future turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:26). Others hold that Israel and the church stay distinct in God's plan, and that God's promises to the Jewish people as a nation are still to be kept. Others stress that God's covenant with the Jewish people still stands, and debate what that means for Christian witness. These notes do not choose among them.

All of them must reckon with Paul, a Jew writing to a mostly Gentile church: “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1), and “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). He warned Gentile believers, “do not boast over those branches” (Romans 11:18). In 1965 the Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council said that ‘the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures’ (Nostra Aetate 4), and many Protestant churches have said the same. The warning in this parable falls first on those who lead Christ's church today.
passages.asks: The tenants wanted the vineyard for themselves. They forgot it was never theirs. Ask what God has put in your care: a family, a gift, a church, a job. Do you treat it as his, and give him the fruit? And notice that the leaders passed sentence on the tenants without seeing themselves in the story. Ask where you might be doing the same.
